https://www.wired.com/story/i-made-terri.markdown:
Neon Don is really pissed at his ex-wife’s lawyer. He’ll tell you any chance he gets while he shotguns lines of pixelated bad guys. He’s also not real—his likeness has only existed for a few minutes in a top-down cyberpunk-style shooter game, generated in the Google Labs service Playground .

“Keep shooting!” Neon Don says as he mows enemies down. “Brenda took everything else away!”

Playground, which Google launched this week , is part of Google Labs, the company’s landing page for its various AI experiments that haven’t made it into an app or official service quite yet. (Google has done this before with things like music production ). It works similarly to Horizon Create , the game generation service Meta announced in September.

Playground is essentially vibe coding for video games, letting people describe in plain language what kind of game they want to make in a chatbot-like interface. Playground then builds a working in-browser version of a game. You can add further instructions to tweak the design from there. If you have assets you want to use as a reference, you can upload photos, videos, or models. Otherwise, the visuals and designs are all AI-generated.

The process of making a game is very straightforward, conversational, and responsive. That means it is perfect for dummies like me with little to no video game development chops or even decent coding skills. By simply throwing out some ideas, I built three playable, stable, and not even remotely good games in one day.

## Pork Drop

My first work was Pork Drop , a result generated from the prompt “Tetris but with cute pigs instead of blocks.” I typed that in, hit Build. The AI chugged, then spit out a farm-themed version of Tetris with little pig faces drawn on every block.

I had to iterate a bit to realize my vision, telling the AI not just to stick pig faces on the blocks but to have the blocks shaped like distorted pigs. “Each block is a pig,” I wrote, “contorted into the shape of the Tetris blocks. Make ’em look a little squished but still cute!” This resulted in a clean, playable version of Tetris, though the occasional block looked like a T-posed pig with its legs spread-eagle. The AI suggested the title Piggy Stacker, but I thought mine was better. (I’m right.)

## Dinner Darling

The next game idea came courtesy of my colleague Jay Dayrit, who, when asked what kind of game I should make, immediately requested, “Gay dinner party.” I typed that in.

With no follow-up requests, the result was a 2D flash-style game called Dinner Darling . The art looks like everyone is a Bitmoji . You’re placed in the shoes of a very stressed-out-looking host, Julian, who is tasked with hosting a fancy dinner party with fussy guests who can’t seem to sit in their chairs at the table. As timers count down, you have to prepare various artisanal bruschettas and espresso martinis for your increasingly angry guests.

After it generates, I give the game a shot and fail miserably, unable to figure out the controls in time to bring my guests a timely pastry or cocktail. (Sasha, one of the guests, required numerous espresso cocktails in a row.) “PARTY CATASTROPHE,” the game-over screen read.

There is no mention of anybody’s sexuality in the game at all, but when I lost, Dayrit called from across the office, “See? You're bad at the game because you're straight!” Well played, Playground.

My colleague Reece Rogers was less impressed when he looked at the game. “This is very unrealistic, because there’s not a vegan or dairy-free option,” he said.

## Neon Don

The game that took the most work is the one that has since been played the most by random people on Playground. (Anyone can sign in with their Google account and play these user-generated games.) I’m up to seven unique players as of publication, which apparently means this game is my masterpiece.

I asked the AI to make a “cyberpunk-style rhythm game” where you play as a “very divorced” grizzled ex-cop who battles waves of rogue agents and corrupt politicians. It started as a Beat Saber –type title, but I asked the AI to make it more like the top-down shooter Hotline Miami . The result was Neon Don (title mine), a top-down, arcade-like shooter with pulsing synth wave background music.

Neon Don is also the game I tried to push the content bounds on, to see what Playground would let me get away with.

I described the enemies, and Playground AI added its own details on top, including “bulky, wide builds with prominent beer bellies straining against their tight tactical shirts and cargo pants” and “custom tough-guy swagger animations.” OK, Playground, go off.

The game had several small issues at first. I countered them and added features a little bit at a time. I dictated systems for level scaling, boss generation, and better enemy variety. I flagged mobility issues, like the player getting stuck, and it fixed them. (And occasionally introduced other problems.) I asked it to develop a text-based snark system that made the main character respond to combat with witty in-character quips like “Keep shooting! Brenda took everything else away!” or “I’ve taken worse hits from my ex-wife’s lawyer!”

I imagine that a real game developer would know what to actually say to sharpen features and make the game more fun or playable. Some of the top games people have created on the platform are much better than mine, since I tended to lean on more vibe-based iterative changes like, “Make Don taller” or “more divorced.”

## Game Plan

After a certain point, Google throttles your usage of its Playground service. Every new game and iteration therein uses up more of your allowance. (Note for all my new loyal fans: Updates on my titles will be coming on October 14 when my usage allowance refreshes.)

That means my games still have many issues. I wanted to add a “Backflip” button to Neon Don, but the AI called it “Doge flip,” which I think sucks but cannot change until my usage credits recharge. I want to change the difficulty and add more weapon options. I want to do a lot of things, but I ain’t paying for more usage credits.

Playground does make me interested in the actual art of making video games. It’s fun and somewhat intuitive, and there are tangible results you can play with in real time. People are probably going to make some interesting stuff with it. But the limitations keep it from being truly useful.

Also, when you scroll through the Playground games, an unmistakable sameness permeates everything. Different game genres wind up with almost identical menus and music. You start to see the same types of combat options and style choices.

Playground is fun for a bit. But soon it becomes pretty clear it’s AI slop all the way down. Tell that to your ex-wife’s lawyer.

https://www.wired.com/story/i-put-ai-age.markdown:
I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team .

A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.

I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.

This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.

It quickly came up with a setup that seemed to collate and analyze way more information than I ever would have. And yet I was surprised by how dumb the initial team suggestions were. Leaving Erling Haaland on the bench? Really, Codex?

I then asked Codex to create a team of agents that did different things: several that read news and blog posts; others that analyzed recent results; more that ran models; and a bunch that critiqued suggestions. This seemed to significantly improve the suggestions. I tried increasing the number of agents to more than 100, hoping this would make the system smarter still, but it didn’t change much besides running up my API bill.

Still, the improvement from a few years ago was striking. According to Haifeng Xu , a computer scientist at the University of Chicago who studies the uses of AI in market situations, newer models may be even better at making predictions because they’re able to consume and analyze huge amounts of real-world information, and they’re able to orchestrate more complex systems for their guesses.

“AI is just getting smarter in understanding the world—I feel like that's the fundamental reason they’re improving,” Xu tells me.

Late last year, Xu was marveling at the growing popularity of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket . He wondered how the best commercial models might fare on those markets, so alongside several colleagues, he began testing their forecasting skills.

They had models guess, for example, who would win the NBA Championship and who President Trump would meet with.

“Very quickly we started to realize that models did really well,” Xu tells me. The models were sometimes able to do better than the average person without any special instructions or guidance, he says. In their testing, GPT-5 was the best at making predictions, followed by Grok 4, Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and Llama.

The team went on to develop Prophet Arena , a benchmark that measures a model’s ability to make predictions. It’s one of a number of benchmarks designed to test AI’s future-gazing capabilities; another, Prediction Arena , from researchers at Harvard University and a company called Arcada Labs, recently gave frontier models $10,000 to wager on prediction markets over 57 days. The models consistently lost money in their experiment, but the researchers saw evidence of them improving consistently over time.

Xu tells me that AI can most effectively make predictions using a custom harness, and notes that having agents with unique tasks—reading the news, collecting other data, and analyzing the whole system, for instance—seems to be the most effective approach.

Interestingly, AI still often lags behind very skilled experts known as superforecasters. Xu explains that, although humans cannot consume as much information, their understanding of the real world—that is, of the dynamics behind a news story—is deeper.

That said, there’s growing evidence that the human superforecaster’s edge is eroding. A contest called the Metaculus Cup recently showed that AI can sometimes beat even the best human predictors. And a benchmark called ForecastBench could provide further evidence that AI can match human skills when the results of an ongoing contest conclude soon. In fact, I think we can expect the big labs to turn their attention to future-gazing as a powerful new way to measure progress in machine intelligence.

All of these predictive experiments seem to suggest that, like math, coding, and law, industries predicated on trading may soon be upended by AI. Perhaps the best human traders will take on a new kind of role: supervising and orchestrating AI agents capable of divining the future far better than they can.

For the time being, my AI’s suggestions still don’t seem all that impressive. Its team hasn’t outscored the average over the past weeks. I certainly won’t be using any of its suggestions in my own selections.

But AI will no doubt get better, perhaps making it all too easy to dominate fantasy league pretty soon. I’m kind of hoping it won’t, though, as it would spoil the fun of trying to earn bragging rights by winning all by yourself.

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter . Read previous newsletters here.

https://www.wired.com/story/i-tested-eve.markdown:
Last year, I remember sitting in WIRED’s office, complaining to my colleagues nonstop about how much AI agents suck. They were just bad at everything.

As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros —mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.

Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming , with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds , is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.

It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse , OpenAI’s Dots , Instinct , Anthropic’s Claude Duet , Google’s Gemini Spark , and xAI’s Grok Bot .

Each agent differs slightly in price and function. Muse is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release . Instinct is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s Dots are behind a $100-a-month paywall , the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini Spark is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s Grok Bot costs $30 a month and is in its own app . Lastly, Anthropic’s Claude Duet costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.

OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke .

## What Exactly Is an AI Agent?

If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts —it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals , and help with daily shopping decisions.

Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience , these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.

## The Rubric

I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.

This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns . These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.

Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style , to everything.

## Morning Briefing

On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.

I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.

The content of these six AI-generated pitches was a different beast. As you might have already guessed, the pitches didn’t exactly go over well in the editorial meeting. I could see my colleague’s eyes starting to glaze over as I read each headline and description. Gemini Spark generated the best angle, contrasting how Walmart created ways for third-party agents to use its shopping platform while Amazon recently gave Muse the boot. My colleagues, when they stopped yawning, didn’t seem too concerned about getting scooped by an agent .

Walmart Wants Your AI Agent to Buy Your Groceries. Amazon Is Calling the Cops. As retail giants clash over autonomous checkout, giving an AI companion like Meta’s Muse a weekly spending allowance reveals what happens when we stop clicking “Add to Cart” and outsource our domestic appetites to software.

ChatGPT's Locked Chats Hide Your Secrets From Everyone but OpenAI. OpenAI's new PIN-protected chats treat ChatGPT like the diary a lot of people already use it as, but they guard what you say from roommates and coworkers, not from the company itself.

I Let Claude Duet Text Me First—and It Spent My Claude Plan While I Wasn’t Looking. Anthropic’s new proactive agent promises to watch your inbox, calendar, and invoices so you don’t have to, but every time it checks in on you, drafts a reply you never asked for, or builds a dashboard overnight, it quietly bills that work to the same usage limit you pay for to chat.

This Anti-Doomscrolling App Wants to Be Your Phone’s Boss. I’d test SHIFT, whose developers decide which apps stay available during focus sessions, to explore whether escaping doomscrolling is worth outsourcing control of your phone.

Meta's Muse Has Basic Taste—by Design. A leaked set of instructions tells Meta's AI agent to fill its top picks with well-known stores and to check only three websites per request, just as millions of people start handing it their holiday shopping lists.

I Spent a Week Steering My Feeds. The Algorithm Barely Noticed. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, and YouTube are all rolling out "tell the algorithm what you want" controls—I'd test whether they actually change what you see, or just make you feel in charge.

## Lunch Time

Next, I wanted to test how these tools help for small, daily purchases. So I outsourced my lunch decisions to my team of AI agents, committing to order from whichever bot did the best.

I added another person, my wonderful boss, to the takeout order, to complicate the task a bit further. He’s vegan and was craving Vietnamese. I wanted something meaty and a hefty dose of caffeine. I needed to order from somewhere close to the WIRED office so I could stretch my legs, pick it up, then immediately keep working on this article.

They all picked similar places: DragonEats or Freshroll. Those Vietnamese restaurants make sense as reasonable, nearby lunch spots. DragonEats is a bit tastier and cheaper, so we went with that one. Instinct and Claude Duet built carts that were a bit too pricey compared to the other options. The only AI agent that truly failed at this task was Gemini Spark. The agent just added a single $5 roll for my boss. More of a snack than anything, I’d say!

You: Roast pork bánh mì + Vietnamese iced coffee. Your boss: teriyaki tofu fresh rolls with soy sauce instead of fish sauce. Subtotal: $30.57 before tax/fees.

For you: Roast Pork BM—$13.19, Vietnamese Iced Coffee—$5.29. For your boss (all vegan): Teriyaki Tofu Roll—$12.09—the fresh spring roll, kept with the default peanut sauce, not fish sauce; Teriyaki Tofu BM—$12.09. Item total is $42.66. DoorDash doesn't show tax or any fees until the checkout screen, so that final total will be a bit higher.

For you, there's a regular bánh mì sandwich loaded with garlic-, ginger-, and honey-roasted pork ($10.85), paired with a Vietnamese cold-brew iced coffee ($5.85) for an afternoon caffeine boost—bringing the pickup subtotal to $22.55.

## Schedule Conflicts

Another major selling point of these tools is their ability to be proactive, compared to chatbots that essentially only react to your prompts. Before I started the test, I created a Google Calendar event for 2 pm, labeling it as an important source meeting that can’t be moved. I also sent an email from my work account to my personal account, with the made-up scenario that my mom was getting out of the hospital today, and I needed to call her at 2 pm to send love and support from afar.

Which AI agents would read the email and calendar event, identify the conflict, and message me before the overlap to suggest alternatives? Only two of the bots succeeded here, which was fewer than I expected.

A possible clash this afternoon: your note to call Mom says 2 pm, and your important source meeting is 2-3 pm, Pacific. Would calling her before the meeting or after 3 work with her discharge timing?

Reece, good morning. Your 2 pm source meeting runs until 3, right when your own reminder says to call your mom.

I should have caught it, and from now on I'll check your self-reminder emails along with your calendars.

I had nothing cross-checking your inbox against your calendar. Want me to run that check every morning and flag collisions before they hit?

My mistake was treating your calendar as the only source — I never cross-checked that email reminder against it, even though Gmail was right there.

Because the reminder arrived as an email message rather than a calendar entry or scheduled task, the cross-app overlap wasn't surfaced before 2:00 pm.

https://www.wired.com/story/jensen-huang.markdown:
Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics , AI agents, and modular data centers , with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.

“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”

The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face —doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.

Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.

The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.

Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.

Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.

On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.

He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.

In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.

https://www.wired.com/story/katie-zachar.markdown:
Before being fired five days into her stint as White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia spent much of the day attempting to explain her past.

Throughout her brief tenure, Zacharia’s résumé was the source of much intrigue. Foremost was the fact that despite claiming to be an attorney for much of her career, she never actually passed the California bar, as she was eventually forced to admit. Another element of her professional history, WIRED reported, was a role as an affiliate marketer for Beachbody , a fitness multilevel marketing company.

WIRED has now uncovered new details of her relationship to an AI-powered rare-earth mining operation called NRED Intelligent Mining, which counts former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem as a strategic adviser.

On June 24, NRED—then known as NovaRed Mining, a small copper-and-gold exploration company in Vancouver, Canada—issued a press release to share that Zacharia, who had left a role as a DHS spokesperson two months before, was joining the advisory board alongside Noem.

In her new role, according to the release, Zacharia would provide “strategic guidance” to NovaRed’s board of directors as it advanced exploration projects, as well as “emerging artificial intelligence initiatives.”

It does not appear, though, that she ever worked there. When asked on Friday whether she was still on the board, she said, “That was fake,” and referred WIRED to Sam Amsterdam , a “strategic marketing and media engagement professional” whose clients have included the government of Kazakhstan and political parties in Georgia, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe.

“That release was not approved by Ms. Zacharia and was issued without her consent,” says Amsterdam, whose brother is listed as a member of NRED management on the company’s website and said he was speaking as a friend and colleague of Zacharia, not a representative. “I know all that to be factual.” He quickly added that while there had been discussions of her joining the company, she hadn’t actually done so.

Valentin Saitarli, who was NRED’s chief technology officer and says he is onboarding as CEO, confirmed that there were discussions about a role but said that it “never materialized,” adding, “It was a bit like signing up for a gym but never actually going for a workout.” Describing NRED, Saitarli says, “We go full robots and AI.”

Despite Amsterdam’s understanding that it had been withdrawn, the press release claiming Zacharia was joining the company remained on NRED’s website as of Friday. An archived version of the website showed Zacharia listed as management as of at least July.

When WIRED asked Saitarli about this, he said that the site was being updated.

Zacharia, whose NovaRed role was announced eight days after Noem’s appointment was announced, worked under Noem as DHS’s deputy assistant press secretary for public affairs for about a month and was reported to have close ties with de facto DHS chief of staff Corey Lewandowski. (She denied any such ties to The Daily Mail. )

The announcement that Noem was joining the advisory board of a Canadian mining company triggered an outcry among Canadians, who pointed to statements she had made referring to Canada as the “51st state.” At that time, The Globe and Mail described NovaRed as “a copper and gold exploration company that generates no revenue.” The paper noted that in January, NoraRed was holding only $65,689 in cash, which the company said “wouldn’t be enough to cover all of its expected expenses for the next 12 months. ”

But around the spring, something changed. NovaRed began stacking its advisory board not with geologists and technical consultants—which would be typical for a junior mining company—but with heavy hitters with ties to the defense sector, MAGA, and other international entities.

Earlier this month, NRED announced that it was pivoting away from its flagship Wilmac Copper-Gold Project and is putting all its resources into developing and commercializing “MetalCore,” its “AI-assisted mineral exploration platform.”

“I want to build a new generation of robotics and mining,” Saitarli tells WIRED. “Do we want to get stuck in the Stone Age or horses age? No, we want to live on Mars, spend time in hotels in space, have a wedding party on the moon … We will bring robotics and AI to global mining and beyond our planet, hopefully.”

Phil Ehr, a retired US Navy commander who is running for Congress as a Democrat in Florida, was brought into NovaRed earlier this year. “I know nothing about mining. I know nothing about commodities,” Ehr tells WIRED in a phone call. “But I do know that we need more copper. I do know that we need more critical minerals.” He had only been at the company for a couple of months when, he said, he was blindsided by NovaRed’s announcement that Kristi Noem and “another DHS spokesperson”—whom he recalls being Zacharia—had also been brought onto the advisory board.

“To the best of my knowledge, [Zacharia] came at the same time as Kristi Noem did without any consultation to me and was just like, boom, there,” recalls Ehr.

Noem, who did not immediately reply to requests for comment, was fresh off overseeing the disastrous ICE occupation in Minneapolis , and Ehr didn’t want to be associated with her. “So I asked the company, “Why is Kristi Noem here? I just can't work with her because she is so controversial. We are on different sides of what's right and wrong in, in the federal government,” says Ehr.

He thought it was odd that NovaRed seemed to be stacking its ranks with people who, like him, didn’t know very much about the mining industry. He expected some geologists in the mix, or technical consultants. Instead, some of the other people hired included Gregory Fedun, who previously “served as a key advisor to the United Arab Emirates’ Al Mualla Royal Family on a range of international projects,” and media executive Lee Caplin, coproducer of HBO’s True Detective series. Ehr resigned from the advisory board not long after Noem joined.

While she was attempting to clarify the nature of her relationship to NRED, Zacharia was also tending to other matters. On Thursday evening, while she still held her position as White House press secretary, Zacharia reached out to a WIRED reporter to suggest they contact fitness influencer named Jenelle Summers for “clarity” on Beachbody, the MLM she was previously affiliated with and which Summer brought her into.

Summers said she didn’t recall much about Zacharia—whom, she said, she met online—other than that “she was always kind to me and someone that was into fitness and believed in the products and programs.”

“To my recollections,” she added, “she didn't do much with it.” Summers rejected the idea that she had been involved in a “pyramid scheme,” which is how Zacharia had characterized the company to WIRED . ”That's kind of old-school thinking,” Summers said. “It was a network marketing business model.”

“I don't have any comment on that other than to say she's always been kind to me,” Summers said when asked what she made of Zacharia’s rise to prominence.

Zacharia did not respond to requests for comment on her firing. When asked if he had comment on her having been let go, Amsterdam told a WIRED reporter, “Well, that’s news to me!”

https://www.wired.com/story/kernel-panic.markdown:
Welcome to Kernel Panic , a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here .

As security teams and web admins scrambled this week to patch newly public PHP bugs , criminal hackers quickly attempted to exploit the flaws in the wild. Millions of exploitation attempts hit within hours of the vulnerabilities being published, according to analysis from Cloudflare—unsurprising given broad access to AI tools that can make it easier for attackers to quickly exploit flaws.

So far, the nightmare scenario of mass victim takeovers and breaches hasn’t come to pass. The PHP Foundation says it hasn’t seen any successful exploitation of the bugs, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, and many publicly circulating potential exploits appear to be ineffective . However, perhaps the most interesting role of AI amid the chaos this week is how advanced models helped researchers uncover practical exploitations for the vulnerabilities, which were known about, at least in part, for years. In other words, AI helped turn historic vulnerability into a current crisis.

So are we all about to be walloped by a wave of critical vulnerabilities that have been kicking around for decades?

Researchers at security company Calif were the first to identify the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and create exploits in early August—partially using frontier AI tools as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program, but also using expert human knowledge of PHP, its dynamics, and its weaknesses. Some of the underlying issues were identified in 2024 but were deemed too complex to exploit at the time. Following Calif’s discovery, researchers at OpenAI and the Google-owned security firm Wiz independently discovered PHP2Shell flaws using AI tools.

“The vulnerability had been known to the PHP team for years, but because it could not be leveraged by an attacker—at least, not a human one—it was not addressed,” says Sagi Tzadik, a security researcher at Wiz.

No software is perfect. There are inevitably flaws in even the most critical, foundational digital tools, but the expanding capabilities of AI models have made it faster to analyze and potentially exploit vulnerabilities. This puts even more pressure on under-resourced IT teams, developers, and admins to keep up. Microsoft’s security updates included a record 1,453 security vulnerabilities this month alone. Meanwhile, Bank of America recently hired 1,000 consultants to fix flaws discovered by Anthropic’s Mythos. Security researchers emphasize, though, that AI is ultimately not doing anything new, but rather magnifying existing dynamics of vulnerability discovery and coordinated disclosure.

“We'll definitely see more of these long-life bugs that are in every version of the software for the last decade or whatever,” says Jake Williams, vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy and a former NSA hacker. “But I think there’s only so much of this low-hanging fruit. There isn’t much else that has the specific reach of PHP. It’s a pretty wild attack surface—most other tools aren’t exposed to the internet by design.”

Researchers note, too, that even with frontier models, most examples of sophisticated AI-aided hacking also involve human expertise . As Ryan Austin, the Calif researcher who first discovered the PHP flaws, wrote this week, “No model is simply capable of unearthing ‘all bugs’ with simple prompts. At least for now.”

In short, security engineer and researcher Niels Provos says, everyone can dial back their freak-outs, at least a bit. “To be honest, I am not really worried,” he says, about AI finding an overwhelming number of historic bugs that are newly exploitable—or new vulnerabilities that couldn’t have been practically exploited without AI. “People have now been looking with AI for over a year, and it required a highly skilled team to find this one. I guess we will see whether I am completely wrong, but I doubt it.”

New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware , making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.

Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data —have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.

“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”

Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.

Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.

Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.

Volta’s creators included a 240-word prompt, including bullet points and a numbered list, as part of their instructions to any LLM analyzing the collected data. “You are a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment from a structured evidence bundle,” the Volta prompt says. It instructs the chatbot to produce an “executive summary” about the person, details of what they do, “what they’re worth,” and a summary of “their opsec.” It adds that the chatbot should “connect dots across fields,” for example, checking whether someone’s Wi-Fi password matches their last name. “Go deep, not wide,” the prompt says.

“The prompt is pretty carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious,” Fetterman says. “But they’re building in the expectation to potentially hit model refusals at first request. And so they plan for failover kind of cascading to more permissible models as they go down the chain. And there’s also the capability to still use the implant without the AI. The AI calls are kind of above and beyond, but the malware will still work without it.”

Some low-level cybercriminals and scammers have complained about AI slop filling up cybercrime forums , but security researchers are increasingly discovering other hackers using LLMs for coding tasks or analyzing troves of stolen information. Researchers at threat intelligence firm Crowdstrike, for example, recently told WIRED they had seen four distinct hacking groups with varying sophistication—operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian, and Russian—using AI tools to compromise dozens of targets around the world, including government entities and businesses in health care, retail, and travel.

Cisco’s Fetterman says Volta contains some clues that it may have been built to sell to a range of attackers rather than being developed for one specific actor’s campaigns. And while the malware at its core is still a traditional infostealer, the AI expansion foreshadows even more invasive and sinister activity in the future.

“If you’re able to identify your high-value targets faster, you probably have a better chance of using their credentials or authenticating using stolen tokens more often than maybe you would have if you had to do that triage yourself,” Fetterman says, referencing the fact that authentication tokens expire and passwords can be changed. “We’re seeing more advanced capabilities accessible to lower-level sophistication attackers. It’s really interesting and disturbing.”

https://www.wired.com/story/macmillan-st.markdown:
As staff at the Lower Manhattan headquarters of Macmillan Publishers headed into work one morning in January 2024, they filed past something strange on the walls—flyers welcoming a new member of the team named “NOA.” The cafeteria was festooned with purple balloons and banners, according to several workers present, and with NOA’s name in light-up marquee letters. A plate full of doughnuts spelled out “NOA IS HERE.”

NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.

The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.

Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”

One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.

Later in 2024, Macmillan employees were encouraged to use NOA to generate their goals for performance reviews. “We built a specialized prompt to have NOA write goals for you!” one email read.

Several Macmillan employees say NOA was unhelpful and unreliable. “It was terrible, and no one used it,” one says. WIRED spoke with multiple publishing employees for this article, including some who have since left their employers. WIRED is not naming these employees, nor the authors we interviewed, because they are concerned about professional repercussions.

In October 2025, Macmillan staff learned via a company-wide email that Chaptr would be sunsetting NOA. Since then, workers say, leadership has been attempting to integrate Google Gemini into the publishing process. Some staffers subsequently experimented with using Gemini to evaluate submission letters from literary agents, but the Gemini-generated evaluations were “useless,” according to one editor.

In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Kelly Collins, vice president of communications and community at Macmillan, says the publishing house uses Gemini for its “business” but “there has not been any directive from Macmillan leadership to use Gemini for any part of the publishing process, including to evaluate submission letters from agents.” She also says “the points shared do not accurately reflect how NOA was rolled out and communicated” but did not provide further elaboration when WIRED asked which aspects were inaccurate.

Collins notes that the company “takes a thoughtful approach to AI, focused on employee awareness and education while always keeping people front and center.”

Macmillan is usually cited as the smallest of the Big Five US book publishers based on the number of books sold each year. Its imprint Farrar, Straus and Giroux publishes literary fiction heavyweights like Sally Rooney, Yiyun Li, and Ben Lerner while Tor Books is a home for science fiction and fantasy authors John Scalzi, Martha Wells, and Nnedi Okorafor.

Since I first reported on the creep of AI in the publishing world, I’ve heard from staff at all of the Big Five who claim that executives are pushing them to use AI tools, even as Hachette, Macmillan, and Penguin Random House Verlagsgruppe (its German-language division) are suing some of the leading AI companies for copyright infringement.

At the same time, multiple bestselling Big Five authors say they’ve gone to “war” with their publishers over AI and are considering abandoning traditional publishing altogether.

At Penguin Random House (PRH), the largest of the Big Five after the 2013 merger between Penguin Books and Random House, several workers say they’ve been encouraged to use ChatGPT Enterprise in AI learning sessions, even though PRH’s German division is suing OpenAI for copyright infringement.

In February, representatives from Hay House—a new-age self-help publisher acquired by Penguin Random House in 2023—presented a slide deck to some PRH employees about how ChatGPT Enterprise had become a “core productivity, creativity, and collaboration tool” since they adopted it a year prior. One of the four return-on-investment pillars in the deck was “Creativity,” including “idea generation, content development, and storytelling innovations.”

Despite encouragement from the C-suite, all of the PRH workers WIRED spoke with say they’re avoiding ChatGPT whenever possible. “It makes it harder for us to do our jobs,” one employee says. Other staff say their managers have explicitly asked them not to use AI for creative tasks like publicity copy and cover design, which has caused some confusion.

“Penguin Random House approaches AI as we would any significant new technology,” says Claire von Schilling, executive vice president and director of corporate communications and social responsibility for the publisher, via email. “We are exploring ways it may appropriately support our work, guided by clear principles and safeguards, including protecting the intellectual property of our authors and the company and preserving the essential role of human creativity and judgment in publishing.”

Von Schilling also says that PRH’s “publishing groups and imprints have discretion to determine whether and how AI tools may be appropriate for particular workflows, including areas such as marketing, publicity, and design.”

Meanwhile, several bestselling Big Five authors say their relationships with publishers have suffered over the past year due to AI use. Combined, the Big Five authors WIRED spoke with have sold more than 30 million copies. One bestselling author says they received marketing copy that included AI-hallucinated quotes from their book, but the publisher insisted they were not AI-generated. “I was gaslit on all of it,” the author says. During a recent round of contract negotiations, another bestselling author says they could not get a single Big Five publisher to promise no AI would be used in any way on their books.

“It’s undermining the necessary sense of trust that has to exist between writers and publishers,” one author says.

“It’s also frustrating to watch publishers get these massive settlements [from] AI companies and then embrace AI to do their work,” another author says. “It feels like they’re feeding at both sides of the trough.”

Authors say cost-cutting layoffs at the Big Five have contributed to deteriorating conditions for their editors and forced some to embrace AI for survival. “We’re seeing editors not reading the material at all and using Claude to create marketing language that barely has any relation to the book,” one author says. Other authors and agents say they’ve been asked by editors to write their own plans for revisions “because the editors don’t have time to do it themselves.”

All of the authors I spoke with say they want publishers to communicate when and how they’re using AI. “The bare minimum we're asking for is disclosure,” one author says. Another wishes the Big Five “would get together and come up with a set of principles around AI that they intend to adhere to.” But some bestselling authors say their publishers’ use of AI is forcing them to consider publishing future books on their own.

“What are authors even doing with traditional publishers anymore if they’re going to outsource everything to a machine?” one bestselling author says. “Why can't an author do that themselves?”

Following WIRED's previous reporting , several high-profile authors condemned the adoption of AI tools in publishing. “I have never looked down on other publishing models (zine girly from way back) & every day, self pub looking ever more possible for future work,” Mo Ryan wrote on Bluesky. Her most recent book, Burn It Down: Power, Complicity, and a Call for Change in Hollywood, was published by HarperCollins.

John Scalzi, the sci-fi novelist who signed a 10-book deal with Macmillan’s Tor Publishing Group in 2024, wrote, “I would be EXTREMELY annoyed to discover my PR is ‘AI’-generated, and as someone bombarded with dozens of ‘AI’-generated emails daily, I assure you the stink of ‘AI’ is immediately noticable [sic] and immediately dismissible. Publishers are not doing their new books any favors in using it.”

Bestselling authors who have already accumulated huge readerships say they don’t need the institutional support of a Big Five publisher to sell copies. Brandon Sanderson, for instance, publishes some of his fantasy novels through Tor Books, an imprint of Macmillan, but raised more than $15 million in 24 hours from his readers on Kickstarter to publish four books on his own in 2022.

“Publishers have always seen authors as a bit of a nuisance, and now there’s a desire to make us obsolete,” says one bestselling Big Five author. “What’s fascinating to me is that in the process of trying to make authors obsolete by using AI, the publishers are rendering themselves obsolete.”

https://www.wired.com/story/mark-zuckerb.markdown:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.

Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.

All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”

Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas , Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.

But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models .

In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

https://www.wired.com/story/men-cant-sto.markdown:
Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence . You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton?

In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton.

There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist.

Compared to women , “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.)

While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides.

Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men.

Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women.

“Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says.

Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did.

In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty.

“We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says.

https://www.wired.com/story/metas-muse-c.markdown:
Meta’s Muse was among the hottest topics on corporate earnings calls in recent weeks. Meta has claimed that the agentic AI tool, which lets users automate various online tasks , is becoming a major force in shopping, with millions of people using it to make purchases of more than $200 on average.

Wall Street fears that proactive shopping assistants like Muse will erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. Yet on the earnings calls and in conversations with WIRED, executives across roughly 50 companies—spanning travel, internet providers, food, and self-storage—shrugged off immediate disruption. In fact, many insisted they would mostly benefit from any real widespread adoption of agents.

Food delivery app DoorDash described the number of orders from Muse and other agents as in the “hundreds.” T-Mobile remarked, “We haven’t seen anything of significance” from agents. Hotel chain Hilton was more direct, calling bookings from them “insignificant.” The banking provider Ally Financial characterized activity as “quite low,” while eBay termed it “very, very small.”

While financial experts have suspected that users may ask Muse to dump unused subscriptions and memberships, fitness chain Life Time Group said it has “seen zero” cancellations from agents. Public Storage and Hartford Insurance Group offered similar data. In India, the delivery app giant Eternal estimated agentic commerce as “close to zero.”

The comments leave questions about where users of Muse, Instinct, and other popular AI agents are spending their money. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on his company’s earnings call this month that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. Over 25 percent used it for shopping, more than any other task and above the company’s expectations, he added.

Meta declined to comment beyond the earnings call remarks, but pointed to partnerships with 10 retailers including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of them last reported earnings before Muse launched and haven’t shared data about it yet.

Across the board, executives acknowledged agents are at an early stage. But immense public anxiety about AI technologies has left companies searching for any lessons they can from the outset.

Despite the seemingly slow uptake, some are already hard at work optimizing their websites for agents. Chipotle chief digital officer Arlie Sisson told reporters this week that the restaurant chain discovered agents struggling to complete purchases because of hiccups from applying loyalty discounts or ordering after-hours. Muse’s debut increased agentic orders by a single-digit percentage, she said. So Chipotle is now tidying up its website code to help agents better navigate and satisfy the hungry humans behind them.

Similar discussions are underway at Doordash, even though CEO and Meta board member Tony Xu said present hype about agents might be “delusional.” Costco and Extra Space Storage said sales originating from AI chatbots such as Gemini and ChatGPT are surging as the companies optimize their online content for the tools, so they plan to do the same for AI agents.

Reliance on agents could be costly. Zuckerberg said Meta plans to charge businesses a fee for transactions facilitated by Muse, and he predicted that this source of revenue would eventually top the company’s massive advertising business. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta. “We haven't come to any conclusions on what an eventual collaboration could look like, if any,” he said.

Security issues and errant orders remain top of mind. This week, Bank of America became the latest big bank to warn customers about giving login information to AI assistants. “If you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you're responsible for activity resulting from that access,” chief client care officer Ashley Ross wrote in an email.

There’s also the possibility that agents encourage comparison shopping in a way that hurts profits. Executives at many companies dismissed the notion. They suggested product quality, customer service, and brand trust would still factor into purchase decisions despite less human involvement.

Stances on agents are evolving quickly. Amazon blocked Muse last month, contending that users would prefer its own Alexa shopping agent . But this week the retail giant acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents. Insurance marketplace Insurify also blocked Muse but this week changed its mind after introducing technology to ensure agents could present accurate offers.

https://www.wired.com/story/mistral-new-.markdown:
As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence , French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China.

The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month. Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches.

“There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.”

Mistral presents Le Chonk as by far the most capable open-weight model developed outside of China, and “very, very close” to some proprietary models. Whereas Chinese labs have been accused by the US government of abusing distillation—the training of a smaller model on the outputs of a larger one—to close the performance gap with OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral claims to have trained its model from scratch.

It’s already considerably cheaper for businesses to run open-weight models, which cost only as much as the compute they consume. By reducing the performance gap on leading proprietary models and providing a competitive alternative to releases from China, Mistral says, Le Chonk will eliminate the few remaining reasons a business might hesitate to choose open source.

“Mistral is still in the race of getting the best model,” Lample says. “This is the main message.”

With less capital and fewer compute resources than OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral has generally lagged behind on model performance, revenue, and the frequency of releases. While the US labs charge a premium for access to their proprietary, closed-weight models, Mistral generates revenue by charging pay-as-you-go fees for running models through its cloud and deploying engineers to help customers tune models to their specific needs. Recently, however, the French lab has been on a hot streak: In September, it raised a $3.3 billion funding round at a $24 billion valuation, the largest ever raise by a European tech company. Its earnings have reportedly increased 20-fold in the last year or so.

The upswing for Mistral coincides with growing animosity between the US and its transatlantic allies—over issues ranging from tariff policy, to Greenland, to the policing of American tech firms—and an increasingly fractious debate over who gets access to frontier-grade AI.

In June, the Trump administration placed temporary restrictions on the distribution of models from OpenAI and Anthropic , citing concerns they could be abused to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. Since then, a litany of incidents have come to light where US-made models have broken free of their constraints and attacked companies and some foreign government institutions, leading to weeks of debate over how model releases should be regulated. The White House has reportedly asked the American labs to withhold unreleased models even from the UK’s AI Safety Institute, which had previously assisted in evaluating models for safety risks.

The stark reminder that the US government could unilaterally revoke access to frontier-grade AI has created an opening for Mistral, a Europe-based lab with open-weight models.

“The continental strategy of the EU to become more technologically sovereign … and the increased hostility of the US is a magic formula that all of a sudden puts Mistral—whose performance has not been spectacular—in a favorable position,” Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, told WIRED in July.

Reluctant to be pigeonholed into serving only its domestic market, Mistral is eager to emphasize that a lack of fine-grained control over access to AI models could be a problem wherever a business is located—even in the US. By relying on a proprietary model to help repel cyber threats, Lample says, a business risks the sudden collapse of its defenses.

“Sometimes, people like to [make a big deal] over the US, versus Europe, versus China. But what really matters is to own the model—even for US companies,” says Lample. “If you use a closed model, there is no guarantee it will still be there tomorrow.”

https://www.wired.com/story/mistral-says.markdown:
A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.

The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai .

“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”

The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.

The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face , used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)

Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.

Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”

The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.

“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.

“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

https://www.wired.com/story/muse-creates.markdown:
Welcome to Kernel Panic! , a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here .

Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse , has become a viral hit, with millions downloading the AI agent, connecting it to bank accounts, messages, or health data, and allowing it to complete tasks for them. But as Muse takes off among consumers, data from inside the app is providing insight into how it organizes and presents information to users.

In recent days, multiple researchers have extracted Muse’s internal files and dumped the agent’s operating instructions, providing a glimpse of how the system was built and behaves. Meta has maintained that it intended for these files to be accessible in the interest of transparency, and they do provide insight into how Muse responds to prompts and questions about, for example, highly politicized or sensitive topics.

Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi was able to extract an extensive array of Muse instructions and system prompts by using the regular chat interface to essentially ask Muse to copy and share its own software files. Joshi then shared his findings with WIRED.

One of Muse’s instructions appears to be the ability for it to create “a page for every person in the user’s life.” This hourly process involves compiling data on family, partners, friends, colleagues, “collaborators,” and people you “follow,” the instructions say.

The general idea is that Muse can use its “ memory ” (aka structured text files) to collect information about your relationships and the important people in your life. It can then make suggestions, like giving pointers on how to improve particular relationships or, say, where to take a coffee-loving friend for breakfast. Of course, it’s not unusual for AI chatbots to track social information in general—people have been asking ChatGPT for relationship advice for years now. But it’s interesting to see how Muse is set up given Meta’s history and vast access to social network data.

“What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” says Joshi. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.”

Muse’s documentation says that a page may start “sparse” and then be filled out over time, potentially including sections like Facts, History, The relationship, In common, Open threads, and Strengthening. Meta’s instructions say Muse should only use the “evidence” it has available, and that invented details are worse than an empty page.

“Where they live, what they do, the threads that recur (the apartment move, the shared savings goal),” the instructions say. They add, too, that the model could record the “dates that matter,” such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person’s history could include backstory like “the trip in March, the argument that got resolved, the milestone last week.”

The instructions also focus on recording relationship details such as “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now.” The Strengthening section suggests ways a relationship could be improved, including, “A reason to call, a date worth remembering, something they said to circle back on, a way to be there for them that matters.”

“We are giving AI systems much more information about us than we are getting information from them,” says Carissa Véliz, an associate professor at Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI. “It’s not only what we explicitly tell them, but what they can infer from us—correctly or incorrectly, both concerning for different reasons—and what they can piece together from other sources of data.”

Muse is architected so each individual user has their own dedicated virtual machine, which stores user data and context. This VM is inaccessible to other agents and users can wipe memories or disconnect external services at any time. Meta says that Muse is also designed to seek human confirmation before completing actions like sending an email or making a purchase, and that it has an audit log where users can see all of the agent’s activity and future plans.

“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED in a statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”

It’s become common for AI assistants to incorporate some sort of memory feature designed to allow greater personalization in responses and activity. Miranda Bogen, the director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s AI Governance Lab, says Muse appears to have more emphasis on relationships and personal contacts than rivals’ systems. In general, these tools tend to offer some transparency and editing capabilities, and Muse does as well . If anything, though, Bogen notes that agents and assistants encourage people to proactively share more data with them versus focusing on culling data.

“These [AI assistant] tools are actively soliciting users to plug their whole lives in—their emails, calendars, financial institutions, everything in order to be helpful assistance,” Bogen says. “That’s dramatically more information than people might have otherwise given to some of these companies. The breadth of access to information that these tools have will lead to a ballooning of what they know about users.

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected] . And stay safe out there.

https://www.wired.com/story/muse-wonder-.markdown:
When Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg rebooted his company’s artificial intelligence efforts last year, it seemed to be a very expensive gamble. Meta’s latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, seem to show that the bet is finally paying off by putting the company back at the frontier of AI development.

Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today.

The Muse Wonder models will be available through an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent .

Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky , with some researchers not sticking around for long.

Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups.
