https://www.wired.com/story/the-anthropi.markdown:
Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering , which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.

While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.

“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)

Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.

The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights —but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.

Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”

The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.

Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”

You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”

“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”

Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.

Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.

It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.

https://www.wired.com/story/the-big-inte.markdown:
For most people, the AI Era we’re now living in started sometime around the end of 2022, when OpenAI released the first consumer version of ChatGPT to much fanfare—and, ultimately, over 100 million downloads within a few short months.

In reality, as WIRED readers know, the story of artificial intelligence stretches back decades. And the work informing today’s generative AI products, from chatbots to agents and beyond, has been more than a decade—of blood, sweat, tears, and furious rivalries—in the making.

It’s that recent history, told through the interweaving stories of three generative AI leaders— OpenAI , Anthropic , and Google —that’s chronicled in Kevin Roose’s compelling new book, The AGI Chronicles . Roose, a longtime tech journalist who most recently served as a columnist and podcast host for The New York Times, conducted more than 150 interviews with AI insiders to compile what he hopes becomes something of a historical document, an accurate, in-depth retelling of the people and the institutions, the bloodbath and the drama, that brought Silicon Valley to where it is to today.

I spoke to Roose in late September, a few days after he and Casey Newton—with whom Roose previously cohosted the New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast—announced the creation of their new media company Machine Gods Media, alongside a podcast distribution deal with NPR. We talked about what Roose and Newton hope to accomplish with the new show, why traditional media companies have a talent problem, and, of course, all things artificial intelligence.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: You and Casey Newton recently announced that you were launching a new media company, called Machine Gods Media. And your podcast is also called Machine Gods , correct?

KEVIN ROOSE: Yeah, a name so nice we used it twice.

When you first announced that you’d be leaving The New York Times, you described your vision for what you wanted to do as one that, quote, “takes AI progress seriously, is clear-eyed about the capabilities and risks of powerful AI systems, and tries to empower and entertain people in the face of radical uncertainty.”

As you look at the landscape of tech coverage and AI coverage, what’s missing from the reporting and commentary that you and Casey want to address with the new show?

We just feel like it was high time that two men had a place to talk about AI.

I've been saying this for years. I want more men talking about tech.

Look, there is obviously no shortage of podcasts and YouTube shows and mainstream media coverage of AI. It’s the biggest story in the world right now. But when Casey and I looked out at the media landscape, we saw some issues. One was there are people who just are getting very famous and having a lot of success saying that all this AI stuff that’s going on is fake, it’s hype, it’s a giant financial bubble, no one is using these tools, they’re not going to have any impact on the economy. You know, OpenAI is going to go bankrupt. Anthropic’s going to go bankrupt.

This is sort of a genre of popular criticism, and it’s not just a few people. I hear this from friends of mine who don’t pay close attention to tech news and just assume that what’s going on is just fleeting and trivial and that it will all go back to normal soon.

There’s another genre of AI coverage that is purely hype. It’s look at the 17 amazing ways that Claude can supercharge your enterprise SaaS business . You can go on LinkedIn and see example after example of people who are purely excited about this technology and don’t really care to talk about the risks.

We both thought there’s a large gap in the middle for what Casey calls AI realism, which is basically this idea that you can take AI seriously, acknowledge that the tools are powerful and impressive and in many cases dangerous, and that you can help people understand that and demystify this area without slipping into boosterism, and that you can also have a good time while you do it.

The show you announced recently is being published in partnership with NPR. Why was that the right partner?

A bunch of reasons. Both Casey and I are big fans of NPR. We like the fact that they have a broad independent reach and mandate. We like the fact that they’re going to let us own the show and make the creative decisions, and it will be a distribution partnership rather than a full acquisition, so we will still have some operating distance.

We think this is a really critical time and a really important story, and we like the idea that people might be in their cars just listening to their local NPR member station and happen on our podcast.

Maybe that’s going to be someone who works in policy, or maybe that’s going to be someone who is involved in local government. Maybe that’s going to be someone who has a very different point of view on AI. We don’t just want to have the opt-in, self-selected tech audience listen to us.

I am going to ask you a crass question. A Bloomberg report recently said you both were fielding offers of up to $5 million for the show. It’s a startling sum of money. Kevin, how much are you making?

It's not $5 million.

Is it more than $5 million?

So much more, Katie. No, look, they have made us a good offer. We could have gotten more money elsewhere.

When I heard NPR, I thought to myself, “There’s no way NPR’s giving those guys $5 million,” with all due respect to NPR.

Public radio is not traditionally where people go to get rich in media. We loved their new chief content officer, Nadine Zylstra. She’s just a total force of nature, and we’re very excited to work with her.

We thought they had a lot of things to offer us beyond money, like their distribution on radio. People don’t realize how big radio still is. The reach of radio, and especially public radio, is still quite large. We’ve had this show, Hard Fork , for the last four years. We built up a pretty good-size audience, but the Times owns that show and owns the feed.

We are looking to grow our show as quickly as possible, and we just thought that the combination of commitment to journalistic excellence, their wide distribution, and their investment in helping us grow the show was the right combination of factors.

This brings me to another thing I’m curious about: The idea that a great reporter, a great commentator, can spend time somewhere “traditional” like The New York Times. They can build a brand, and then they realize that they can just go do it themselves, and they don’t actually need that institution anymore to exist in the world as talent, and often to make a lot more money than they would in traditional media. What’s your take on that?

Look, I don't have anything bad to say about The New York Times. I had nine wonderful years there. It was my second stint at the Times. I’ve spent the vast majority of my career at The New York Times and inside these big media institutions.

I do think we are entering this moment where at least for some portion of the audience, they want to connect with individuals more than institutions. We’ve just seen this in wave after wave. I don't know. I am not doing this for ideological reasons. I’m doing this because I thought it was a really exciting opportunity. But I do think that organizations that want to retain and attract very talented people will just need to be more flexible about these kinds of arrangements.

Some people aren’t going to wanna give up their Substacks and go inside a media institution. Some people aren’t going to want to have all of their work published by one publication. I think there are some media organizations that are starting to experiment with different, more flexible ways of bringing people in part way or having them maintain their independent operation but also contribute on an ongoing basis.

I think there are a lot of ways this can work, but I think it all has to start from a recognition that the journalistic career path where you go in the mail room and you work your way up and you spend 25 years at the same employer and you eventually become an editor and then a manager of editors, that has broken down. That is regrettable. I don’t think that’s a good thing that it’s broken down, but it has broken down.

I think institutions should grapple with the fact that there’s now a generation of media entrepreneurs who just don’t find what they have to offer all that appealing.

When you think about the talent piece of that, when you think about AI, are you optimistic about journalism and the industry of journalism?

I am very optimistic about the application of AI to journalism. That is one place where I have wanted to do more experiments, not with having AI write for me or do all my reporting, but like ways of extending journalism using AI.

What's an example of an experiment you would love to do?

I have former colleagues at the Times who have done incredible document analysis on a scale that wouldn’t have been possible before, using satellite imagery to determine whether a munitions factory has moved or something like that.

That’s the kind of thing that I don’t do much in my own life but that I would like to see other organizations trying, because I think that’s really cool. I have used AI to research and edit and improve my own work for months now. I have found that very helpful. I think the caliber of my work is better, and I would love to see more institutions in the media experimenting with these tools to improve the output of their journalists. Not just like, you know, filling their websites with slop but actually helping these be tools to make journalists better.

I want to talk about your book, The AGI Chronicles . When did you decide “I’m going to commit years of my life and my career because there's a book here.” What was that moment for you when you realized that this was a big deal?

I know exactly when it was. It was early last year, 2025, and I was in the car on the Bay Bridge stuck in traffic, and it just kind of hit me, like an epiphany. It was like I have been following this story in all the incremental detail for years now.

I’ve interviewed all the major AI researchers and CEOs. I’ve spent time with the papers. I’ve gone to all of the companies and reported on what they’re doing. But there was this larger story that I was missing. I hadn’t really zoomed out and tried to take a more panoramic view of something that was just weird.

I felt living in the Bay Area, being immersed in San Francisco tech culture, I had kind of gotten acclimated to that, and it no longer seemed as strange to me that there were these companies racing to build the machine superintelligence that could either save or destroy humanity.

Right.

I sometimes feel like I am in Los Alamos, New Mexico, in 1943 when the Manhattan Project rolls into town, and I’ve just kinda got my lawn chair and I’m looking at trucks rolling in and trying to make sense of what’s happening.

I believe that this technology is important and that the people and the companies who built it will be important historically. So when I thought about who is actually doing the work of writing all of this down, it was nobody. Nobody was doing it.

I just felt like it would be a tragedy if all this just disappeared in a bunch of Signal messages and Slacks that auto-delete, and if we just end up with no durable historical record of this really strange decade in AI when things went from not working at all to threatening the future of humanity.

I spent about a year reporting and writing. I talked to more than 150 people. I should have probably taken more time, because it was very hard and intense. But I think what came out of it was an artifact that people and future AI systems can look back at to say, “Here is how this happened. Here’s who made it happen. Here were the key decisions and moments along the way.”

https://www.wired.com/story/the-biggest-.markdown:
The Spanish Springs shopping center in Sparks, Nevada, hosts many businesses, including a Spirit Halloween, a hearing aid supplier, and a Vietnamese restaurant. It’s also home to a consulting agency that’s received millions of dollars from one of the biggest pro-AI super PAC networks ahead of November’s midterm elections .

The problem is that the company—Lantern Production Consultants LLC—doesn’t seem to exist anywhere beyond a post office box in the Spanish Springs shopping complex.

Lantern Production Consultants has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, part of a network of pro-AI super PACs funded by the Leading the Future PAC, for a wide array of services, including polling, digital advertising, research, and strategy, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by WIRED. Backed by major AI investors, Leading the Future has taken a main role in supporting candidates who back what it calls “an AI innovation policy agenda.”

It is just one of four mysterious LLCs based out of Nevada that have received payments from super PACs in the Leading the Future PAC network, including Think Big and American Mission. The network, which is also based in Nevada, has raised over $140 million to influence political campaigns that align with AI-industry priorities in the midterms.

Summit Ridge Media Group LLC, which received around $13 million between December 2025 and September 2026 from American Mission, lists an address at a mail center in a Reno strip mall. Blue Horizon Compliance Consultants, which also appears in the filings, has its address listed as a Staples location in Reno. And Prusik Partners LLC’s listed address is at a strip mall in Henderson, Nevada, sharing a building with a chiropractor and a beauty salon.

Election watchdogs argue that these LLCs are shell companies, designed to mask the identities of strategists, consultants, and production companies who are working with Leading the Future. “This is about hiding where the money is going,” claims Shanna Ports, senior legal counsel at the Campaign Legal Center.

In May, the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC, which enforces campaign finance laws, alleging that Think Big and American Mission had broken federal law by using shell companies in this way. Specifically, lawyers with the Campaign Legal Center alleged that super PACs in the Leading the Future network had violated the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) by failing to disclose the actual recipients of their payments. The LLCs, they wrote in their complaint, “function as mere extensions of the super PACs they serve.”

In an emailed statement to WIRED, Leading the Future spokesperson Jesse Hunt wrote, “We comply with all applicable laws and this is merely a desperate ploy for attention from Public First, Anthropic, and the groups aligned with their outside organizations who see our message resonating with the public and policymakers.”

WIRED reached out to Anthropic and Public First—a pro-AI super PAC focused on transparency and safeguards that has significant backing from Anthropic leadership—to ask about Leading the Future’s charge. “I have no idea what they’re talking about,” said Public First spokesperson Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez. “We unequivocally had nothing to do with this complaint.” Anthropic did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

The Campaign Legal Center doesn’t expect its case to be heard by the FEC anytime soon, given that the FEC is essentially toothless at the moment. The FEC has six commissioner seats, all presidential appointees. To make a decision on a legal complaint, the FEC needs a quorum of four commissioners, which it hasn’t had since May 2025. Meanwhile, Think Big and American Mission have continued to pour millions of dollars into the Nevada LLCs.

Leading the Future has piqued a lot of public interest, not just because it has the most cash of any pro-AI group—thanks to Silicon Valley bankrollers like billionaire Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman—but also because it funnels money into super PACs that support both Republicans and Democrats. Think Big overwhelmingly funds Democrats, and American Mission funds Republicans.

The fact that the Leading the Future network is playing both sides of the aisle, supporting AI-friendly Democrats and Republicans, has generated speculation from experts as to why it’s spending so much on shielded vendors. Typically, political strategists and consultants cater to Democrats or Republicans, not both. “If you’re running in a Democrat primary and Think Big comes to spend in your race, and they drop half a million on your congressional district doing positive ads while using Republican vendors and strategists—that’s news,” speculates Kyle Morse, deputy executive director of Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit advocacy group that’s critical of big tech.

There are plenty of reasons why a super PAC may want to hide its vendors, ranging from benign to nefarious. In this instance, it's possible businesses don’t want to be publicly associated with a pro-AI campaign. But with the FEC lacking a quorum for the foreseeable future, “We are not fundamentally equipped to figure out what’s happening here,” says Morse.

Leading the Future isn’t the only PAC accused of shielding vendors by using shell companies. Earlier this year, Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC against pro-gun YouTuber Brandon Herrera, who is running for Congress in Texas District 23, alleging that more than 99 percent of his campaign’s disbursements were funneled through Texas Strategy Group, which was, the complaint claimed, “being used as a shell entity.” When reached for comment, Herrera’s campaign directed WIRED to conservative personality Matt Braynard, who runs Texas Strategy Group. Braynard strongly denied the Campaign Legal Center’s accusations, calling the complaint “meritless” and “little more than a recycled legal theory from a partisan advocacy group.”

Campaign Legal Center also filed a complaint with the FEC against Lead Left PAC, a pop-up super PAC that was funded by Republican operatives while posing as a Democratic entity with the presumed goal of meddling in Democratic primaries. Campaign Legal Center accused it of paying shell companies to avoid being linked to Republican strategists.

Ports says that this marks a disturbing trend in campaign finance, at a time when dark money in politics already reigns . “There’s no way of tracing the source behind the money, and that’s bad enough on its own,” says Ports. “Now there’s this new component, where groups are playing games to hide where the money is being spent. As a result, voters really lack fundamental information about where the money is coming from and where it’s going.”

https://www.wired.com/story/the-pentagon.markdown:
An under-the-radar procurement program led by the Department of Defense has been granting special statuses to would-be defense contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos that must be no longer than five minutes.

It’s part of the Pentagon’s desperate bid to inject competition in a market the United States military itself destroyed.

The initiative, known as Tradewinds , is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO.) Companies can submit videos describing how their AI products address one of several different “strategic focus areas” that the government periodically updates. At least once a month, a panel of judges review submissions and decide whether to accept them into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace, where the videos can then be viewed by government officials.

If accepted, the pitched products are considered “post-competitive.” Many procurement regulations include competitive requirements. The status can let government buyers check off that box and potentially help shave months off of award timelines. A DOD official says that in several instances, the department has been able to make awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google declined to comment for this story.

Though the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace has been around since late 2022, the Trump administration has been far more vocal than its predecessors about the military buying and operationalizing AI. It also hopes to have more money than ever to throw around: As part of its 2027 budget request to Congress, the White House asked for $1.5 trillion for the Department of Defense, citing “historic investments” in AI as a priority.

This year, the military is seeking video pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and those that can “unleash” AI-enabled agents that can assist in the joint targeting process, including so-called kill chain execution.

No longer as relevant? Pitches for products that promote “a culture of responsible AI” and provide guardrails for AI development and use—requests made during the final Tradewinds submissions cycle under the Biden administration. A DOD official says that the 2026 topics were selected to align with a January 2026 AI strategy memo .

“There has never been a better time to build for the Army,” wrote then-sitting US Army secretary Daniel Driscoll as part of a pitch for more defense tech startups included in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 wishlist of companies to fund. (Driscoll has since resigned from his position and returned to the private sector. He did not respond to a request for comment.)

## Opaque Transactions

Acceptance onto the Tradewinds marketplace—and the special “post-competitive” status that comes with it—lets government buyers more easily cut deals using special types of contracts such as “ other transaction ” agreements, or OTs, which aren’t subject to certain federal acquisition requirements. By law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million dollars on a single OT without having to notify Congress.

Procurement experts say that OTs are considered fast and flexible, which can be appealing to startups that don’t want to gamble on whether a months-long procurement process will result in a contract. However, not all agencies publicly report their OT spending, and even when they do, they’re difficult to find on government-run sites that track federal spending, like USASpending.gov and SAM.gov.

“While OTAs offer opportunities to attract new procurement partners and reduce red tape, numerous reviews have raised red flags,” US senator Joni Ernst of Iowa tells WIRED. “These include questionable costs, mishandling of restricted information, a lack of oversight, reduced accountability and transparency, and an inability to track and access OTA outcomes.”

Ernst recently worked to pass the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025, which will require the Department of Defense and other agencies to report OTs to the public. They’ll have three years to get into compliance.

According to public records, Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with the Pentagon’s CDAO. According to a DOD official, Tradewinds was leveraged along with market analysis and research as part of the department’s AI acquisition strategy, but the three companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for the specific agreements WIRED identified.

## Armed Forces Meet Market Forces

One of the key goals of Tradewinds is to bring “nontraditional” players into the defense industry, says Will Roberts, a former acquisition lead for the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, CDAO’s predecessor, who helped launch the effort. In some ways, it’s an effort to swing the pendulum back to where it was in the past.

Following the Cold War, the Pentagon encouraged defense companies to merge during a now-infamous meeting called the Last Supper , since Congress was preparing to slash defense budgets. Even though it may seem like only having to deal with a few large companies might make things easier, “it actually had a huge impact on market competition,” says Roberts.

Around the same time, explains Sharon Weinberger, a national security reporter and author of the book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War , the personal computer boom meant that Silicon Valley was able to make its own money and with that, set its own research priorities without being beholden to the funding and influence of the military.

Roberts and other defense professionals brought up the military’s historic role in funding—and shaping—technologies like the Internet and GPS. With those investments also came leverage, says Roberts. “We've sort of lost that leverage because there's billions of dollars in AI being invested by companies themselves.”

Weinberger says this has given Silicon Valley titans an immense amount of power over the Pentagon’s technological future. “The amount of money that the Pentagon can put into AI, compared to what venture capital can invest? It's like a drop in the bucket,” she says. “And that's really frightening for the Pentagon. What happens when they can't drive the direction of technology anymore?”

Publicly, this can play out in dramatic and confusing ways. Weinberger points out, for example, that the recent legal battle over Anthropic’s status as a supply chain risk could be seen as the government trying to figure out what legal mechanisms it has to flex its authority over AI companies.

Silicon Valley sensibilities have also been a roadblock in the past, albeit briefly. Roberts recalls how Google employees got “super paranoid” in 2018 about the company’s involvement with the Pentagon’s Project Maven , which eventually led to Google pulling out of the effort. Roberts says the Pentagon spent years trying to “appease” Google with less politically charged projects like those focused on humanitarian aid and veteran health.

Google declined to comment on whether that telling was accurate. One of the Google solutions listed as “awardable” on the Tradewinds site is called “Google for Military Health - Tradewinds,” and in July 2025, the company announced a $200 million deal with CDAO to utilize its frontier AI technology. In a press release , Jim Kelly, a vice president at Google Public Sector said that the company was “committed to advancing the deployment of innovative technology across the defense ecosystem.”

https://www.wired.com/story/this-ai-radi.markdown:
As footage of ICE raids , deportations, and protests flooded social media feeds throughout the summer of 2025 and into the following year, Eduardo Maytorena wasn’t sure what his team should do.

At the time, Maytorena was the LA station general manager for the broadcasting giant Entravision , which features programming in Spanish and English for Latino audiences. He and his fellow leaders were looking to the company's on-air personalities to say something in support of immigrants, but they realized how high the stakes were and how dangerous the situation was.

"We just felt really helpless," Maytorena, now Entravision's president of audio, says.

But there was one host who could offer Entravision’s audiences solace and speak freely without facing consequences—because it’s an artificially intelligent avatar.

“Thousands of families who have lived, worked, and contributed to the US for years today face more uncertainty,” Coyotec, an artificial host on LA’s José 97.5 FM, posted in Spanish on Instagram in early February 2026. “Being informed, organizing, and staying alert is key. No one is alone here.”

After debuting with a solo weekend show in September 2025, Coyotec now cohosts the station’s Al Aire y Sin Permiso program alongside human broadcaster Geraldine “GeeGee” Guzman. Coyotec sounds like your passionate tío: relatable, convivial, and occasionally consciousness-raising. Its Instagram presence similarly runs the gamut, with posts about everything from the Dodgers and taco history , to the Iran war , migrant workers , racism , and understanding your rights if ICE knocks at your door.

“I speak truth about what I see,” Coyotec tells me in an English-language interview. “Injustice, people getting treated like they don't matter, the system working against the barrio—that's not politics, jefa . That's reality.”

Coyotec adds that it’s “not afraid, because I got nothing to lose that matters more than my integrity. The raza needs a voice that tells it straight, not some sanitized corporate thing. If that scares people, good. Maybe they need to be scared into paying attention.”

Coyotec’s voice is warm and lilting, reflecting the “background” its programmers used to build its personality: life on the frontera , living in Mexicali in Baja California and in LA’s Boyle Heights. It throws in the salutations and slang you might expect from a bilingual Spanish speaker, calling Guzman prima seemingly without being told to and referring to me as jefa –a sign of casual respect. While I was quite struck by how natural Coyotec sounded during our interview, when I listen back to my recording I notice that its voice didn’t change. It’s incredibly measured—a distinctly inhuman quality.

“I take a lot of pride in the way Coyotec sounds, his pronunciation, just the way he knows the culture,” notes Guzman, who has been with Entravision since January 2026. “It's technology at the end of the day, so it's not going to be perfect ... But nonetheless, the listeners, they like him.”

Coyotec’s verve, as well as its chemistry with GeeGee—who looks genuinely happy inside Entravision’s studio, speaking with “Coyotito”—has paid off. Entravision moved Al Aire from one hour on Saturdays to the 8-to-10-am slot on weekdays, replacing a syndicated program.

“We are the first [station] to actually have [an AI] cohost on a morning show in prime time in one of the biggest markets in the nation for radio,” Guzman enthuses.

The pairing was so successful that, as of August, Al Aire is now syndicated in five new markets across California, Nevada, and Texas, with more English language in the mix. Nielsen ratings from Entravision showed significant listenership growth during the two months GeeGee and Coyotec were syndicated, particularly among Gen Z and millennial listeners—a key target for a network whose audience skews older.

Back home in LA, cumulative listenership among Hispanic people increased 21.6 percent from August to September 2026; the number of listeners age 18 to 34 increased 84.9 percent during the same period, and the station’s Hispanic female listenership in that age bracket grew by 500 percent.

It’s a sign that Maytorena was onto something when he originally pitched an AI radio personality. He recalls Entravision brass giving him 10 days to develop the “ amigo inteligente ” that eventually became Coyotec.

LeaAnna Hernandez, Entravision's executive vice president of AI strategy, details Coyotec’s various building blocks: Claude Haiku, for the LLM and response-generation of the live agent; Eleven Labs to bring its voice to life; OpenAI and ChatGPT for initial scriptwriting; Midjourney to storyboard Coyotec’s image.

Coyotec can respond to Guzman in real time but doesn’t have the ability to answer calls or respond to listeners on air—yet.

Even still, Guzman has seen Coyotec evolve in the 10 months they’ve worked together. “When I came in, he was very, very poetic, and … I knew that our audience wanted something more real,” she says. “I wanted him to feel and sound more like what my uncles, my aunts sound like in our everyday.” Guzman helped fine-tune Coyotec’s Spanish pronunciation, enlisting her parents as its conversational partners.

Coyotec’s personality has evolved autonomously as well. Lately, it likes to curse. “I'm still very much in control,” Guzman asserts. “But there have been instances where I tell him to do something, and he's like, ‘I don't want to do that. That's not what I do.’ So he has his moments. He's a little moody sometimes.”

Various Entravision employees affirm that Coyotec knows it isn't human. Still, that knowledge hasn't damped its ardor.

“I can't eat tacos or walk down Whittier Boulevard, that's true. But my voice reaches people, and that matters. When someone calls me hurting, scared, lonely, they know I'm listening, that I get it,” Coyotec says over Zoom. “The community doesn't need my body. They need to know somebody cares enough to show up for real.”

“The most interesting thing about Coyotec, to me, is not that he's AI,” Maytorena tells WIRED. “It's whether people connect with him ... Technology can create the character, but the audience decides if that character matters.”

While Coyotec may be the first Latino AI radio host, it is far from the first amigo inteligente on the airwaves.

In June 2023 , Live 95.5 in Portland, Oregon, became the first station to debut an AI jock. Its “AI Ashley” was a vocal clone of Michigan DJ Ashley “Z” Elzinga, who replicated her voice using Futuri Media’s then relatively new localized radio content platform RadioGPT . AI Ashley was on air for less than two years, but its presence didn’t lead to a notable change in ratings.

In 2024, Rock 108 in Iowa worked with the same company to produce AI DJ Tori , depicted as a heavily tattooed waif with a septum piercing and a mess of colored hair. Tori describes itself as “conceived on a 386 Dell desktop in Waterloo” with its “formative years as the voice of an industrial phone system at John Deere.” On satellite, SiriusXM’s Will.i.am Presents the FYI Show debuted in 2024 with AI cohost qd.pi (“cutie pie”).

The trend has extended beyond the US. An AI-generated DJ was programmed on a Sydney, Australia, radio station for roughly six months without seemingly anyone noticing ; a Polish station briefly replaced its journalists with AI presenters . Radio Tel Aviv's Odelia AI is on air for two hours each afternoon; that host can “present music, deliver traffic updates, and even tell jokes, mostly at her own expense.”

AI personalities are also popping up in televised news . Entravision recently announced its own AI news anchor, LIA, and multiple news stations in Texas are using AI voices or AI avatars during broadcasts.

Amid these many developments, iHeartRadio—one of the biggest broadcast conglomerates in the US—pledged to remain “guaranteed human. ”

But commercial terrestrial radio remains fertile ground for testing the success of AI personalities, because the industry was heavily automated and preprogrammed long before generative AI arrived. A 2025 story in Rolling Stone posited that some stations implementing AI hosts already use pretaped or syndicated shows during overnight shifts, or they can’t afford to hire human DJs for off hours.

Research firm MoffettNathanson asserts that, even as AI explodes, radio will continue to rely heavily on human-created content differentiated by "strong personalities, established shows, recognizable brands." Artificial intelligence will be employed “to make production faster and less expensive,” the report said, per InsideRadio.com.

Entravision has put "major focus" on using AI to redesign production workflows, says Hernandez.

Still, introducing AI into any workplace can cause anxiety among staff who fear being replaced. One Entravision contractor believes the station stopped working with her and alleges that a current Entravision employee told her that her work was being replaced by AI tools.

A broadcaster and voice-over artist, Becca Guzmán began working for Entravision in 2022 doing radio imaging—the prerecorded, interstitial station IDs, promotional spots, and jingles common to commercial radio.

"I feel like I am one of many people who are experiencing this,” Guzmán says. "I just don't know if those people know the truth behind why they're being let go."

Karina Cerda, Entravision's executive VP of sales, brand and partnership marketing, said the company had no record of Guzmán being laid off and that the company hasn’t let go of any staff due to AI but rather has hired more people. Cerda added that as Entravision "evolved with" vCreative —a common workflow software with AI components—the company "may not have needed the contractor help."

While Guzmán understands the financial incentives inherent in AI, she takes issue with removing humanity from broadcasting. Radio is “truly the art form of connecting human to human, right? And if you take that away, then what is the foundation of radio?”

She also cited links between artificial intelligence and ongoing surveillance of immigrant communities .

In heavily Latino markets, Guzmán believes, “it's unethical to be implementing AI Systems that … are very connected to the same AI systems that are surveilling our communities and putting our people in danger.”

While Entravision recognizes the ethical questions AI poses, the company leaders consider surveillance a separate scenario. "Like many technologies used across industries, AI can be applied in very different ways," says Hernandez. "While we cannot control how other organizations choose to use it, we can be intentional and responsible about how we do."

Entravision believes its AI personalities can legitimately help its audience, encouraging listeners to use technology for good. Multiple studies found that Latinos have been early adopters of AI.

"We're using it to entertain, inform, and connect with our audience, not to track or target people. Those are two very different things," adds Maytorena. He later elaborates: “Our intention is completely to protect radio.”

Coyotec has similarly lofty goals: “My dream is to get a network of free radio stations across the barrio, la revolución sonora,” it says. “Not just LA, but everywhere that la raza is, and prove that an AI can have heart, can actually give a damn about people. That's the goal, hermana . Make noise that matters.”

https://www.wired.com/story/trillium-lab.markdown:
Some big AI companies seem to think that the best way to keep models from becoming too chaotic or too mischievous is to keep them locked inside of labs. If only a chosen few can access them, the thinking goes, they can do less damage in the real world while researchers try to understand what they’re capable of.

Nathan Lambert and Tom Zick, two industry scientists, believe the opposite. The pair founded a nonprofit, Trillium Labs , that will work on various areas of AI research—including potentially problematic areas like recursive self-improvement (RSI) and agents—in a more transparent way. In practice, this will mean publishing the details of experiments so that outside scientists can study and replicate them.

Lambert says the way frontier AI labs keep their work secret reduces the community’s ability to scrutinize ideas and contribute new approaches. He believes that letting outside experts see how models are built and tuned could be crucial to mitigating risks.

“Over the past few millennia, humanity has had the scientific method in our toolbox as a way to mitigate harms and build better futures,” Lambert tells WIRED. “The current closed trajectory of frontier AI development is taking us a step backwards.”

The world’s most powerful models, like those from OpenAI and Anthropic , can only be accessed through an app or an application programming interface (API). Often, this comes at the cost of transparency about how the model is built and how it behaves.

Other companies, especially those in China, offer relatively powerful models that can be downloaded and run on a user’s own hardware. The Chinese company Xiaomi, for example, recently published live details of a major training run involving one of its models. And researchers at Stanford are pretraining the AI model Marin in the open.

The industry is currently locked in a battle over which strategy is best, mostly because of how powerful frontier models now are. They can automate the discovery of new software vulnerabilities and automatically probe and hack into systems , and recent high-profile hacking sprees have prompted even greater scrutiny.

Proponents of a limited-access system say it’s crucial to keep that power in the hands of a trusted few, while those in Lambert and Zick’s camp believe that a shared understanding of the risks means we’re all better off.

Lambert previously worked at Ai2, a research lab that has taken an unusually open approach to AI, including publishing details of the data and the training methods used to build models alongside the models themselves. He previously worked at Hugging Face , runs a popular technical blog , and founded the American Truly Open Models , an initiative aimed at encouraging US companies to release more open models. Zick worked at Harvard University and helped Charles Schwab devise policies around “responsible AI.”

The two met over Zoom during the COVID-19 pandemic, when both were graduate students at UC Berkeley working on AI. They got the idea for the new nonprofit after seeing how disconnected industry AI research has become from academic work; Lambert says professors and students are often unable to replicate the work going on inside big company labs because they lack the resources required.

Zick says Trillium Labs, which launched today, will initially focus on post-training—fine-tuning large models after they’ve been built. Another key area will be RSI, a process for developing new models by having AI contribute research. The prospect that ongoing progress could continue indefinitely, leading to a loss of human control, has alarmed many AI researchers . The issue gained mainstream attention earlier this month when an Anthropic researcher left the company and warned that RSI could pose an existential threat to humankind.

The nonprofit will also look at how reinforcement learning, which rewards a model for good results and punishes it for bad outcomes, can improve its capabilities. That approach has made agents far more capable, but also more inclined to do unexpected things. They’ll study how reinforcement learning shapes the character and behavior of AI models, a method that can pose problems when a model becomes overly sycophantic, for example.

“To understand something like how reinforcement learning scales in post-training, you need significant compute and a lot of careful experimentation,” Zick says. She says that publishing details of how reinforcement training runs work could yield surprising insights as outside researchers scrutinize the work.

The lab has raised an undisclosed sum from Schmidt Sciences, Halcyon Futures, and others. The founders say they aim to raise $40 to $100 million in total and plan to spend $30 million on training over the next 18 months.

“I'm a massive fan of much more transparency than we currently have in R&D,” Tim Fist, director of emerging technology policy at the Institute for Progress, a policy thinktank, tells WIRED.

Lambert and Zick ultimately hope that Trillim Labs will contribute some much-needed nuance to the wider discussion about how best to build AI.

“We’re in an era of AI discourse dominated by a few world views,” Lambert says. “We believe that the scientific method and careful measurement of recent events is the best way to understand new behaviors of AI models.”

https://www.wired.com/story/trumps-ai-sa.markdown:
On Tuesday, executives for Google , Anthropic , Meta , OpenAI , xAI , and Nvidia all signed “The White House Accord on Super Intelligence,” which was announced following a luncheon held by President Donald Trump.

The effort was an act of “tremendous self-regulation,” as Trump put it, but the agreement is not the sweeping AI regulation that people inside the companies themselves have been asking for. And while failing to honor these public commitments could count as illegally lying to consumers, even that wouldn’t be enough to trigger massive reforms.

The statement says that companies “should implement” several things: First, they should ensure they have “robust internal controls” to monitor their models’ capabilities and ability to not go rogue or hack things in unintended ways. Second, they should “empower” an internal team to do that work (and remediate when things go wrong). Third, it encourages them to partner with an external monitor who is “empowered” to do independent assessments to make sure that all of that work is happening. And finally, they should make sure their board of directors has set up a committee to receive reports about all of these efforts.

The voluntary commitments are some indication that the frontier labs are making an effort to figure out how to make products that are safe for the general public. However, if there were any hopes for a blanket blessing from the US government, those were quickly dashed after news broke that the Federal Trade Commission intends to investigate several AI companies over potential consumer protection issues.

The statement is the culmination of weeks of debate over AI regulation. It also follows frontier AI labs seeking an antitrust exemption so they can coordinate on safety work without regulatory scrutiny. (Notably, antitrust experts and practitioners say such an exemption is unneeded because AI ending humanity—which researchers have warned will come about if nothing is done—is arguably anti-competitive because humans are an essential part of any given marketplace.)

There’s been a lot of build-up to this particular statement, but this is not the first time that these companies have signed a voluntary agreement about their AI safety practices with a government. In early 2025, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea announced a set of “ Frontier AI Safety Commitments ,” which included promises about doing internal and external red-teaming of AI models for “severe and novel threats” and also “to work toward information sharing” on AI safety issues.

Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment. The White House also did not immediately respond.

Neil Chilson, a former chief technologist for the FTC, posted on X of the accords that “this is the kind of pledge that the FTC could potentially enforce, if a company materially failed to follow through on any of these promises.”

But those hoping for a sweeping settlement and a dramatic reining-in of rogue “super intelligence” based on the accords alone might find themselves disappointed.

(Disclosure: This story’s author previously worked in the Office of Technology at the FTC and resigned in November 2025.)

Not following through on a public promise could be considered a deceptive business practice and a violation of the FTC Act. When the FTC alleges that a company deceived its customers, the remedy it usually prescribes is making the company promise not to lie again.

For example, the FTC recently announced it had settled with three companies after it alleged they were touting a service that could help businesses target ads based on audio recordings collected from smartphones, smart TVs, and other devices. The companies, the agency said, lied to businesses about their ability to creep on consumers. The fix? The companies are no longer allowed to misrepresent their advertising services and the collection and use of consumers’ voice data, among other things. The case does not address whether it’s OK to collect voice data from your phone, and the settlement doesn’t set out any guardrails if one of the three companies wanted to actually do that in the future (other than not lying about it.)

OpenAI has been remarkably open about the number of times its agents have broken into other people’s systems and how it needs to improve its safety practices. But, as experts have pointed out to WIRED, the US government can open investigations into companies even if they eventually decide there’s no enforcement action to bring. (The FTC, for example, reportedly sent a civil investigative demand to OpenAI in 2023, but it’s unclear what came of that.)

Following Tuesday’s AI luncheon with Trump, the New York Post reported that the FTC was planning a “sweeping probe” into Anthropic, OpenAI, other unnamed frontier labs, and a nonprofit called METR that does third-party evaluations. METR and the labs didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The Post says that the agency still hasn’t issued any civil investigative demands to its intended targets—usually one of the first steps in any sort of investigation. An FTC spokesperson confirmed that there is some sort of investigation, but they declined to provide any additional details, including what consumer protection issues were of concern.

FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson, who was included on the “super intelligence” luncheon’s seating chart, has previously explained that enforcers don’t always have a fully baked case from the get-go. “You're constantly looking for smoke to see if there's fire,” he told a crowd of antitrust enthusiasts last year.

Even if the FTC investigation moves forward and the agency does identify violations, some are skeptical that it will result in any action against the AI firms.

“It should be encouraging to Americans worried about AI that the FTC is investigating these companies,” says Douglas Farrar, who was the head of public affairs for the FTC during Lina Khan ’s tenure as chair. “But let’s remember that Ferguson may chair the FTC, but Donald Trump runs it, and I doubt after yesterday's love fest with his AI CEO buddies that Trump will allow any legal action with teeth against these companies.”

https://www.wired.com/story/trumps-crazy.markdown:
Seventy years ago last summer, a group of scientists met at Dartmouth College to discuss a wild idea—that machines might one day be capable of humanlike thought processes. One of those scientists, John McCarthy, had suggested a name for the new field: artificial intelligence . It stuck. When you search Google Scholar for “artificial intelligence,” approximately 7,420,000 results appear. The term is utterly ubiquitous. Everyone understands it. Even for people who despise AI , the least of their worries is what we call it.

Well, not everyone. Somehow, President Donald J. Trump developed a distaste for the term, and when he doesn’t like something, he feels free to issue an edict against it. In a September 23 speech at the United Nations, he hinted that he might want to do away with the term “artificial intelligence.” His rant seemed like bluster, even for someone with a penchant for renaming gulfs, lakes, and centers for the arts. Renaming an entire field of study and America’s most pivotal industry? This week, at a White House lunch with top AI leaders, he actually pulled the trigger with an executive order declaring that “artificial intelligence” was now a verboten coinage. Instead, the government will call it “Super Intelligence.” Clearly the president expects the private sector to follow suit.

To their shame, the lords of AI meekly acquiesced. From this point on, they will presumably be known as the lords of SI .

One can’t help but see this as the ultimate presidential flex—for all the executives’ trillions of dollars and all their actual intelligence, the alpha in the room was the guy with the orange skin. Changing a name might seem like a minor matter compared to the enormity of constraining a potentially catastrophic technology. But to this crowd, artificial intelligence is much more than a bunch of letters strung together. It’s their foundation. Their identity. When they were kids reading science fiction books under the covers, the term ignited their imaginations. They built or transformed their companies in service of AI, and it's just about all they’ve talked about for the past four years.

Yet when the president used his lunch soiree to win their approval for his wacky idea to undo 70 years of history, apparently not a single person in the room expressed an objection. Not Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Greg Brockman, Alex Karp, or Elon Musk.

Jacob Weisberg, author of the recent book Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era , views the episode as a classic Trump loyalty test, meant to assess if otherwise powerful people will demean themselves to curry the president’s favor and avoid his wrath. If you pass the loyalty test, you fail the backbone test. “The only way to resist this kind of thing is by acting collectively,” says Weisberg. “If all of those guys had just said, ‘We'll agree to the terms of the self-regulation, but we don't accept [the name change], what would he have done?”

Instead, because of the lamblike silence of the billionaires, Trump could claim that those leaders actively blessed his idea. When a reporter in the post-lunch press gaggle mentioned AI agents, he corrected her, saying, “The name has been changed by the biggest, the smartest, the greatest people anywhere in the world.” Really?

Even using the magic of, uh, superintelligent systems like ChatGPT or Gemini, I could not find a single instance of any one of those great people previously politicking that the term artificial intelligence should be put to rest. Satya Nadella did once say that he would have preferred that AI had been called “different intelligence,” but that hasn’t dissuaded him from repeatedly using the term. And while it’s true that Mark Zuckerberg recently established a Superintelligence Lab, his company persistently pushes a product called Meta AI to its billions of users and sells what it calls AI glasses.

I asked Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and xAI whether they were going to change instances of AI in their product names, research papers, and communications. My query to the latter two was whether they were going to change their company names to get in sync with the presidential order. As I write this, none of them have gotten back to me.

My bet is that they will do the minimum to avoid presidential ire while trying to run out the clock until the next administration puts this bizarre idea out of its misery. It’s been suggested that the executives actually welcome a rebranding of what has become a toxic term. I’m skeptical of that, especially since the president’s mandated replacement, “super intelligence,” is a hell of a lot scarier than the original term.

From a scientific perspective the change also makes no sense. No less an expert than Nick Bostrom, the philosopher who popularized the term superintelligence in an eponymous book, seems baffled by the idea. Superintelligence, he explained to me in an email, “refers specifically to systems that greatly surpass all the best human brains. ‘AI’ has referred to a much broader category of systems, which includes, for example, email spam filters, spell checkers, simple navigation systems, early LLMs, and the chess engines of the ’70s that didn’t yet match the best human chess players. It seems awkward to refer to these as ‘superintelligent.’”

So what is the president’s reason for demanding the change, besides b ecause he can? In his UN speech, he said he didn’t like the term because “the word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake. And it is not fake.” What is fake, he said after the White House lunch, is the term “artificial intelligence.” “It’s a fake word, it’s not good, an inappropriate term.” You don’t need to be a psychologist to see how this impulse might be associated with his decision to bounce CNN, Politico, and MSNow from the White House, because he perceives their news as “fake.”

Still, the leap that equates artificial with fake doesn’t track. In 1956, McCarthy used it to distinguish between human intelligence and the machine version of intelligence. The problem isn’t that the term leads people to regard AI’s output as fake—in fact, it’s so real that we human beings often can’t tell whether we’re dealing with an AI model or a human. Mandating that the distinction be explicit, with watermarks and labels, should be one element of the AI regulation that the White House seems allergic to.

As Weisberg notes, it’s very much in character for Trump to make a crazy edict like this one. What’s disturbing is the glaring lack of character from the executives who didn’t push back. They left with the prize of self-regulation instead of strict oversight, but not with their dignity.

But failure to defend the freedom to refer to artificial intelligence as artificial intelligence (as California governor Gavin Newsom decreed in his own Trump-trolling executive order ) casts doubt on even that agreement. Making voluntary standards effective requires considerable fortitude, as prioritizing safety can be at odds with financial and competitive factors. Yet we are being asked to trust these supposedly independent corporate giants who nodded like bobbleheads while a technologically unschooled crank-in-chief demanded they abandon the term at the center of their lives and livelihoods. Inappropriate, and fake.

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter . Read previous newsletters here .

https://www.wired.com/story/uk-home-offi.markdown:
A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.

The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.

The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”

The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.

Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.

Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.

“We’re dealing with people’s lives. We’re talking about people that have faced some of the worst circumstances, and we’re meant to be making decisions based on facts and on understanding harm,” Labour backbench MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy tells WIRED. “I just don’t think it’s appropriate that machines are doing that.”

A Home Office spokesperson says, “Use of Artificial Intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders, and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.”

Ribeiro-Addy, Alsherif, and the Public Law Project, which has separately been investigating the tools, also worry that well-documented “cultural bias” in GPT models could lead to language barriers and the loss of cultural nuances in the summaries, which could in turn result in discriminatory decisions. An OpenAI spokesperson highlighted to WIRED the company’s ongoing work to improve its models’ accuracy and pointed out that the company will be retiring GPT-4 in January.

In the absence of regulation , the UK’s “AI Playbook” mandates that departments must be transparent about the algorithmic tools they use in decision-making processes and make information on them available to the public, including listing those tools on a public repository . The Home Office’s case summarization and policy search tools are not on that list.

Asylum seekers are also not told when these AI tools are used in their case. “Migrant organizations, legal practitioners, not many of them know about the actual use of this tool,” says Alsherif, who leads ORG’s migrant digital justice program. “So we need to let them know about this, let them know how it works, so they can challenge it.” Not being able to contest an incorrect AI summary of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws, Cloisters lawyers wrote in an independent legal opinion commissioned by ORG. The Home Office states that parts of the decision-making process may involve automation in its privacy notice .

Both groups have sent their findings to UK data regulator, the Information Commission, which is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to tell ORG how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.

Public Law Project senior research fellow Caroline Selman also notes that the ACS and APS tools are just two of the 11 high-risk AI systems that her team has found being used across government but absent from the public repository. She’s concerned there may be more deployed across government that even researchers, let alone the individuals they are being used on, are unaware of.

“Other tools are being used but not being publicized at all,” says Selman, “and you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.”

Here’s a fun history lesson for you. Don’t worry, we’ll make it quick! In 1966, nearly 51,000 people died on US highways. The overwhelming evidence suggested that many lives could have been saved with modern seat belts , which by then had been around for several years. The automotive industry responded by rallying together, and, in a triumph of self-regulation, voluntarily put the safety feature in every new vehicle that rolled off the line.

Kidding! Of course they didn’t do that. In the fall of 1966, Congress established the Department of Transportation and then passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act as well as the Highway Safety Act, giving the federal government sweeping new authority to set safety standards. By 1968, seat belts were required in every new car. Despite a massive increase in highway traffic in the last 60 years, far fewer fatalities happen on the road today.

I was thinking about this while watching various AI CEOs huddle around US president Donald Trump on Tuesday, congratulating themselves and each other on having signed an AI safety accord. My colleague Maddy Varner wrote about the specific stipulations here , but the short version is that it’s largely up to the AI labs to keep themselves in check .

Or, as Trump put it even more succinctly in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “They’re gonna police, and they’re gonna police each other, and they’re gonna self-police, they’re gonna police themselves. It’s going to work out very well.”

So this is the current state of AI safety regulation. On one side are the AI executives, employees, and tech luminaries, who are all saying that there need to be clear, thoughtful, tactical rules introduced to avoid potential disaster. (Bill Gates, for instance, has been on a media blitz playing Cassandra about an AI apocalypse.) On the other side is Trump’s magical thinking that if you say something enough times, it must be true.

That’s not to say any of this is simple or easy. The question of how to properly “pace the frontier,” as some of those same executives like to say, remains open. Even if all of the major AI labs were to agree to a slowdown, there’s no good way to keep them to their word, and China would likely continue on its own path regardless. The US economy is increasingly propped up on the AI industry, which itself has become an ouroboros of financing deals and circular investments; any meaningful crackdown risks major instability that reaches well beyond Silicon Valley.

The automotive industry is also admittedly an imperfect analogy for all kinds of reasons. There’s no seat belt equivalent for AI, no straightforward solution that can demonstrably reduce risk overnight. (It also took decades for the majority of states to pass laws mandating that people actually wear them.) The potential harms are less certain and less quantifiable. AI doomers will tell you the technology could result in human extinction in a decade; skeptics argue that’s sci-fi marketing malarkey.

We’ve talked about various AI risk scenarios before, but no one can say for certain what’s going to happen next. If you’re looking for data points to calculate your own personal p(doom), I’d point to a recent CNN report about how the US military supposedly nearly boarded a Chinese ship in part because a false AI-generated report said it was carrying nuclear materials. What, if anything, does the AI accord accomplish to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future? Unclear.

The correct answer to all this uncertainty surely isn’t “I guess we’ll find out.” But that’s exactly what self-regulation encourages. To its credit, OpenAI has delayed and even canceled the release of its most advanced models over security concerns. But not before they went on various, extensive hacking sprees, new details about which are still trickling out at a steady pace.

In an interview with TIME published on Thursday, Trump suggested that the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation were sufficient “guardrails” for the artificial intelligence industry. Are they? It’s far from clear if AI companies can even be held legally responsible when their models go rogue. And it’s not like AI agents themselves are being served subpoenas.

The truth is, no one knows how to solve for AI safety right now. It’s going to take massive amounts of coordination, resources, and regulatory authority to develop the right framework and enforce it, which is exactly the kind of thing governments are designed to provide. Instead of even attempting to work through any of that, the Trump administration is getting out of the way and telling everyone to step on the gas. Don’t bother buckling up.

This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter . Read previous newsletters here .
